checks: All fibers fit one ball and the mass is finite. Every minimizing sequence is eligible for affine-threshold compactification. At the anchor the threshold always equals t, so the affine realization has t as its value there, even if the anchor fiber has zero volume.

For lower semicontinuity, take a subsequence whose capacity values converge to the liminf, which is finite because masses lie in [0,M]. Compactification of attaining slopes preserves the anchor limit t and the direction u and produces an admissible limiting cap with that mass. For upper semicontinuity, hold one limiting attaining slope fixed. The test masses converge by dominated convergence away from null fiber boundaries. These arguments apply at every anchor and every real t.

Translating a containing cap to a boundary-through-point cap gives a subset. For a vertical through-point cap take any unit u; finiteness of P and boundedness of y−x give one finite L with L|a₀·(w−z)| strictly larger than all relevant continuous terms on bases of nonzero margin. On every vertical boundary base the tilted cap takes a subset of the whole included fiber. The tilted cap contains the point and has no larger mass, regardless of whether the vertical boundary carries positive mass.

Normalization of the continuous component gives the threshold u·x for every nonvertical through-point cap. Continuity on the compact sphere yields an attaining direction, and the finite-slope part realizes it. Uniform continuity on the product of the sphere and K_z proves the fiberwise continuity of the minimum. Finiteness of the fiber union and compactness of each fiber give the global maximum, also when M=0.
